articles.title_orig: Sabalenka knocked out of China Open in straight sets by Bartunkova, Djokovic outlasts Zverev
articles.title_zh: Sabalenka knocked out of China Open in straight sets by Bartunkova, Djokovic outlasts Zverev
articles.content_orig:
Aryna Sabalenka, of Belarus, reacts during the third round of the women's singles match against Nikola Bartunkova, of the Czech Republic, at the China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim)
BEIJING (AP) — Second-ranked Aryna Sabalenka was bundled out in the third round of the China Open in straight sets by the Czech Republic's Nikola Bartunkova on Sunday. In the men’s draw, Novak Djokovic maintained his perfect record at the tournament with a 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 victory over U.S. Open champion Alexander Zverev in the quarterfinals.
The No. 34-ranked Bartunkova defeated the four-time Grand Slam champion 6-4, 6-3 in just over an hour and a half leaving the tournament without its two top seeds in the first week.
Newly crowned world No. 1 Elena Rybakina was ousted from the tournament on Saturday and will now be joined by Sabalenka in exiting WTA-1000 event in Beijing early.
Sabalenka, who was denied a three-peat at the U.S. Open last month by Rybakina, squandered five break points in the first set as her historic struggles in Beijing continued. The 28-year-old Belorussian has never progressed past the quarterfinals at the event.
“First of all, I focused on myself, to be calm,” Bartunkova said. “And Aryna, she’s great, she’s a legend, she’s a Grand Slam champion. So, yeah, I’m really happy that I won the match ... I’m not a girl who celebrates too much.”
Bartunkova will next play 24-year-old Sinja Kraus of Austria, who earlier defeated Dayana Yastremska 6-1, 6-4.
Fifth-ranked Mirra Andreeva eased into the fourth round with a 6-4, 6-1 victory over Polina Kudermetova. This year's French Open winner fired six aces and took five of her seven break point opportunities to overwhelm her Uzbek opponent in just 68 minutes.
Djokovic is bidding to win his seventh China Open title and is now 32-0 in Beijing, eclipsing Rafael Nadal's 31-0 start at the French Open for the best start at a tour-level tournament in the Open era.
The Serb started slowly, dropping his serve in the opening game of the match and eventually losing the first set but bounced back to take the next two to secure the win.
“I gave him an early break and then it was hard to come back in the first set," Djokovic said. “I had a couple of break points when he was serving for the set at 5-4, but didn’t use them, but I kind of felt already from midway through the first set that I was starting to get a good rhythm.”
Djokovic will next face Daniil Medvedev in the semifinals.
Earlier, Hubert Hurkacz beat Karen Khachanov 7-6 (2), 6-2 and will face Alex de Minaur, who beat Andrey Rublev 1-6, 6-2, 6-3, in the other semi.

China said on Sunday (October 4, 2026) that "divergent opinions" fuelled by U.S. tariffs contributed to the lack of agreement on overcapacity and forced labour at the G20.
The United States holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies this year, which also includes China, India, France, Germany and Japan.
Trade ministers held two days of talks this week in Milwaukee, but failed to reach agreements on countering overcapacity and forced labour, criticisms commonly aimed at China.
A draft ministerial statement against excess capacity, seen as driving costs down unfairly, "was supported by all but a handful of members", top U.S. trade official Jamieson Greer said after the talks.
The draft called on all countries to move to eliminate structural excess capacity in their economies, among other actions.
"Issues such as overcapacity and forced labor have been highly controversial since their inception," China's Ministry of Commerce said in a statement on Sunday (October 4).
It said G20 members are subject to tariffs related to forced labour and are "frequently targets" of investigations concerning overcapacity.
"Against this backdrop, many members expressed differing views from various viewpoints regarding the presidency's decision to table these issues and push for the issuance of a joint statement and the establishment of cooperation mechanisms," it said.
"... due to divergent opinions among the majority of members, the meeting failed to produce an outcome document on these topics," it said.
"China has noted that the post-meeting Chair's Statement mentioned that the U.S. side, together with two other G20 nations, issued a statement outside the G20 framework on the issue of forced labor," it added.
The statement did not specify which countries opposed it.
A G20 leaders' summit will be held at a golf resort in Miami owned by U.S. President Donald Trump in mid-December.

articles.title_orig: China’s Getting All the Cool Phone Tech. Where’s My Robot Camera and Rear Screen?
articles.title_zh: China’s Getting All the Cool Phone Tech. Where’s My Robot Camera and Rear Screen?
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Living in the US means getting a great range of cool phones, but some just don’t make it onto store shelves over here. At Snapdragon Summit 2026, I handled a pair of phones that embody the injustice of not getting the cool devices more broadly available in other markets. Where are my cutting-edge phones?
Some blame rests with the peculiar phone payment hegemony run by US carriers, which has primed consumers to pay for their new devices over a few years as part of their monthly mobile service bill. If a new phone brand wants to enter the US market, it pretty much has to be sold through carriers, as OnePlus did and Huawei failed to do. Americans rarely buy their phones at their full price up front.
There are other slight technical reasons, as some of these phones from brands that aren’t established in the US don’t support all the 4G and 5G network bands used by US carriers. And there are political forces at play, as the US ban on Huawei devices has shut it out of the country’s market.
But the end result is that the US misses out on neat phones that I got to try out at Snapdragon Summit, some of which run on the new chips we saw shown off during the keynote. The new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and the 8 Elite Gen 6 pack performance upgrades and new AI boosts to mobile gaming .
Novel phone design doesn’t require top-end silicon (though I’m sure it helps); rather, a handful of phones that head to other countries just have bolder designs. Though I’m still delighted by the passport foldables that have come out this year, like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, there’s something to be said about the phone innovations that won’t reach our shores — but which were tangibly real in my hands.
Rear screens have started cropping up on Chinese phones, and the Xiaomi 18 Pro is the highest-profile device to feature one, which is nestled to the right of its camera block. The phone will run on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chip, while its larger sibling, the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (which we didn’t see at the summit), will use the more powerful Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Both phones have a rear screen.
The moment I held the phone in my hand and saw the rear screen in action, I was hooked. Much like the cover screens on foldables, there’s a limited but potent set of use cases for these small but strategically placed screens. The best advantage is to get a preview of what the main cameras are about to capture, which is a massive help when wanting to use the rear cameras for a selfie — ideal when in a low-light environment in which bigger sensors are needed.
There are other playful and fun use cases for a rear screen, like showing notifications or smaller app widgets. Presumably, you’ll be able to see text previews or info like which song is playing on your media player, which could be helpful if your phone is face down and you don’t want to pick it up to check the whole screen.
Funnily enough, that’s the entire pitch for Google’s HiLight feature on its recent Pixel 11 Pro phones — a small ring around the phone’s rear camera flash that blinks different colors for different kinds of notifications or contacts. Even on its own, I (and others at CNET) felt this was a very weak feature that resembled similar perks from phones years ago. Compared with the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s rear screen, it’s practically prehistoric and wildly less useful.
Where US-designed phones get a colored nightlight, Chinese-designed phones get a small foldable cover screen on their handsets.
“I enjoyed the widgets and animated wallpapers, as well as the upgraded selfie-shooting experience the display unlocks,” said CNET Principal Writer Katie Collins, who saw the Xiaomi 18 Pro at Snapdragon Summit. She was careful to point out that perhaps light-based notification solutions like the Nothing phones’ light glyphs could be healthier for folks trying to avoid screens. Personally, I’d at least like the choice to pick one up in the US.
I also got a chance to see Honor’s famous robot phone, which CNET’s Collins covered at MWC 2026 and saw in-depth on a trip to Guangzhou, China , to see it in detail before it launched in that country. The device has a small camera mounted on a gimbal arm for precise control, kind of like a DJI Osmo Pocket camera that  extends from and retracts into the back of the phone.
As Collins discovered, you can activate the gimbal camera either manually through the camera app or with a hand gesture (though you’ll have to retract the protective transparent sheet covering the camera first). When I got my hands on it at Snapdragon Summit, I cooed at using touch controls to pan the camera around, getting neat angles without having to turn my phone. Naturally, it also arcs up and over the phone for selfies.
“I was impressed with its features and versatility, but more so by Honor’s boldness. It’s the closest thing I can think of in the phone world to the avant-garde,” Collins said of her early hands-on time with the device in China.
Admittedly, the phone is a bit of a gimmick — an overengineered solution to manually shifting a phone’s rear camera, though I would love to get sharp selfies with the 200-megapixel shooter at the end of its gimbal arm. Moreover, it could also theoretically enable the kind of smooth tracking and panning that DJI’s handheld cameras are known for, providing phone photographers more professional options in their pockets. At 9,999 yuan ($1,483) for the version with 12GB of RAM and 12,999 yuan ($1,923) for the 16GB version, the phone isn’t even that much more expensive than Apple or Samsung’s flagship competitors.
However, Honor phones also aren’t sold in the US, and this one isn’t expected to be sold outside of China, so I would have to import the robot phone if I wanted to take it out for a serious spin. The future was only in my hands for a brief moment to test out its most iconic gimbal feature (I didn’t even try out its Yoyo AI assistant), but it was yet another example of Chinese phone experimentation that wouldn’t reach US shores anytime soon.
It reminded me of pop-up cameras like on the 2018 Vivo Nex for rear cameras that flipped to the front like the 2020 Asus Zenfone 7 Pro , which were short-lived attempts to pack more powerful selfie shooters without sacrificing front screen space to punch holes or notches.
Years later, we still don’t have solutions beyond punch holes and dynamic islands. Honor is at least looking forward to something new and different from the flat candybar phones we’ve seen for nearly two decades. Here’s hoping more innovation reaches US shores soon.

articles.title_orig: VIDEO: Instant reaction to Miami's win at Clemson
articles.title_zh: VIDEO: Instant reaction to Miami's win at Clemson
articles.content_orig:
The growing gap between No. 4 Miami and Clemson was on full display in a 41-13 Miami win that provided the clearest picture yet of the shifting power dynamic in the ACC. It also served as a referendum on two wildly different approaches to running a program in 2026.
Dabo Swinney's Clemson Tigers were once the unquestioned dominant force in ACC football, winning eight conference titles in 10 years from 2015-24 along with a pair of national titles. However, change can happen quickly in college football -- especially in the transfer portal and NIL era -- and in short order, Miami has supplanted Clemson as the ACC's best team under Mario Cristobal.
The Hurricanes still have a long way to go to match the same level of dominance over the conference that Clemson showed at its peak — that is, if they remain in the ACC long enough to do so. Miami has yet to reach an ACC Championship Game, much less win eight in a 10-year stretch, but after reaching the national title game last year, the Hurricanes have proven themselves to be one of the nation's elite.
Miami's ascent and Clemson's fall aren't unrelated, and the chasm between the two teams in quality is the direct result of the way the two head coaches have embraced, in Cristobal's case, and resisted, as with Swinney, the changing landscape of college football.
Cristobal was long known as one of the best recruiters in the country as an assistant and later as the head coach at Oregon , but his ability to land commitments from players has now been supercharged by NIL, the transfer portal and a deep-pocketed donor base in Miami.
Few teams have been as aggressive in the transfer portal and NIL space as Miami, and Cristobal has built a roster loaded with talent by combining elite recruiting with transfer portal classes.
Since Cristobal took over in December 2021, Miami has landed a top-10 recruiting class in three of his five years in charge (15th in 2022 and 2025) and a top-10 transfer portal class in each of the last four years (12th in 2022), per 247Sports .
The quarterback position is where the Hurricanes have been particularly aggressive in the portal, spending big to land a top transfer quarterback in each of the last three years -- Cam Ward, Carson Beck and Darian Mensah .
While they're far from the only team to take that approach, no one outside Indiana has had more success portaling in quarterbacks and maximizing their talent in one year. Ward became a No. 1 overall pick, Beck led the Hurricanes to a national title game, and Mensah is one of the Heisman frontrunners midway through the 2026 season.
Clemson was once the team in the ACC that entered every season with loaded rosters. Swinney proved himself to be one of the nation's top recruiters and used to stack top-10 classes, overwhelming opponents with the depth of talent on the sideline.
However, Swinney's efforts at the high school level have steadily dipped, with his last top-10 recruiting class coming in 2021 -- the year before Cristobal arrived in Miami. While the Tigers continued to get the most out of those classes, they've atrophied outside the top 20 in each of the last two years.
The only way that can work is if it's made up for in the portal, but Swinney was famously one of the longest holdouts against the transfer portal, refusing to use it altogether early on and still being slow to embrace it fully.
Swinney's fierce loyalty was once his superpower, but that stubbornness has become Clemson's Achilles heel. The modern game has proven to reward coaches and players alike for making cold, calculated business decisions. Swinney refuses to do so, which could be endearing to the Clemson faithful if it weren't costing them the chance to be competitive for championships.
The Tigers have never had a top-50 transfer portal class, and they are lagging behind the best in college football as a result. That shows up on the field in a game like Saturday night's, where the Hurricanes overwhelmed the Tigers with the kind of size and speed that used to populate the Clemson two-deep.
There is no path back to college football's mountaintop for Clemson without embracing what is required in today's college football. The Tigers only needed to look across the sideline Saturday night to see what that looks like in the form of a Miami team that's surpassed them and is now the ACC power that sets its sights on the Playoff each season.

articles.title_orig: How the Cornell case is affecting women who have experienced sexual assault
articles.title_zh: How the Cornell case is affecting women who have experienced sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
Olivia Petter, who says the Cornell University rape allegations have "triggered" her to recall her own experiences of sexual assault. Olivia Petter hide caption
When Olivia Petter first saw the news about the sexual assault allegations at Cornell University, she was shocked by how familiar parts of the story felt for her.
"The more I found out, the more triggered I became," she said. "I think for me, the worst thing was seeing the group messages that these boys were allegedly sending to each other on the night of the alleged rape."
Reading those exchanges brought the London-based author back to boarding school in England, where she says older boys targeted her and her friends from the age of 13.
"They would walk past us and whisper 'Fresh meat,'" Petter said. "They would rate us out of ten and shout numbers at us when we walked down to the dining hall." Petter says she recalls boys pulling down girls' trousers while they held their lunch trays, humiliating them in the school cafeteria.
After a party, when she was 17, she remembers a boy putting a "hand down my pants" when she was trying to go to sleep. "No preamble. We hadn't been kissing... and I was kind of wriggling, trying to get him to stop."
"The thing that people need to understand is when something like that happens to you, it's really hard to just say, no, get off me, because your body goes into this panic mode," she said. "You freeze and it takes a while for you to understand what's happening."
"There were just so many instances of sexual assault and we didn't really recognize it at the time because we didn't have the language," she said, adding that the culture continued into her time at university.
Petter, now 32, is among those sharing their own experiences online in response to the recent rape allegations that have emerged at a Cornell University fraternity house.
A former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, sued the university and seven former students last month, alleging she was drugged and repeatedly raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, when she was 20 years old. Attorneys for some of the men have denied the accusations.
The case has led to a wider reckoning over attitudes to sexual violence. On social media, many women have been using the hashtag #IamJaneDoe to discuss their own experiences of sexual assault and rape.
The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Monday. Heather Ainsworth/AP hide caption
Other universities have acknowledged the issue, too. As the case has become a national news story, the editorial board of The Daily Pennsylvanian — a student newspaper at the University of Pennsylvania — published a recent piece titled "Penn has a Cornell problem, too."
For some survivors, following the coverage can feel like reliving an earlier assault, says Hannah Braunstein, a Washington D.C. based psychotherapist and trauma specialist. She says stories like these can bring back more than just memories for people who've been sexually assaulted.
"Suddenly, they're inundated with all of this news and then their own experience through memories or body sensation is beginning to unfold for them. It can be absolutely horrifying," Braunstein said. "And it can immediately transport them back in time."
For Erin Smith that reaction was immediate. The yoga instructor and mindfulness coach, who lives in Winchester, Ky., first saw the news about Cornell on social media and immediately searched for more details.
"I was so enraged, I set my phone down and just paced around my kitchen like a caged tiger," Smith recalled. She says the story brought back the physical distress she remembered from being assaulted as a child.
"I had that feeling in my stomach that happened during my experience [when] I was 12," said Smith, who is now 53.
Erin Smith, who says she was "enraged" after reading the Cornell allegations. Katherine Dooros/Katherine Dooros Photography hide caption
Braunstein says repeated exposure to stories like these can intensify emotions. Yet, people may feel compelled to keep reading, hoping more information will help them feel better.
"We keep searching for more information because we think if we understand every detail, then finally we'll feel better internally," she said. "But, often it does the opposite, and keeps people activated internally."
Braunstein recommends using a timer to keep news or social media checks to five minutes a day. When someone feels overwhelmed, she suggests turning their attention to their immediate surroundings.
"One thing I talk about with clients in my office is using first sight, looking around the room and calling out what you see, noticing what you hear," she said. "Feeling your feet on the floor. That's a grounding technique that works."
Smith said she eventually recognized that she needed a break from the comments on social media. Spending time outside, being with her dog and playing guitar has helped her feel calmer. But, she said the anger remains, so she has started to write about it.
Petter also turned to writing. As she continues following the case, she wants to use her anger to start a dialogue around sexual assault.
"I want to hold on to the rage because I think rage is powerful and will enable me to have these conversations with the people in our lives," she said. "And when I say people, I mean men."
Petter says she wants men to have those conversations among themselves, too, and challenge derogatory comments about women within their own friend groups, including online.
For Smith, the Cornell case feels personal because it brings so many survivors of sexual assault back to their own experiences.
"I think that's why so many women are triggered right now, because Jane Doe is all of us." she said. "We all have some sort of story."

articles.title_orig: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.title_zh: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.content_orig:
Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a general election to choose new leaders at the national and regional levels, in a vote that could affect the country’s European Union membership bid.
On Saturday, about 3.4 million voters are choosing the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.
Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a United States-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.
The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric and division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla, ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former president, Milorad Dodik, told the final rally of his right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) in the entity’s capital Banja Luka late on Friday.
In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
The EU granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska.
This general election is the first in the country in which new electronic tools are being used to scan ballot papers and carry out biometric fingerprint verification in a move to reduce fraud during the election.
Polls close at 7pm (17:00 GMT) and first results are expected later on Sunday.

articles.title_orig: Yemen leader announces major military operations against Iran-backed Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemen leader announces major military operations against Iran-backed Houthis
articles.content_orig:
The Saudi-backed government of Yemen on Sunday announced a major military campaign against the Houthi militia, a key Iranian ally, plunging the Middle East even deeper into war.
In a televised speech, Rashad al-Alimi, the leader of the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government, said that the government was seeking to reclaim all the territory it had lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years.
The government and the Houthis have been engaged in fierce battles in recent weeks, after the Iran-allied militia took control of the country’s Red Sea coast, increasing pressure on shipping routes and energy markets unsettled by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
The Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which supports government financially and militarily, have also attacked each other directly.
Mr. al-Alimi’s announcement appeared to eliminate any hope that a truce would be reached. In his speech, he said that the government’s military operations would continue “until the country is liberated.”
The Houthis also say that they are fighting to liberate Yemen, and have dismissed government fighters as Saudi mercenaries. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said in a statement on Sunday that the group’s fighters “will not stop carrying out further painful operations against the Saudi enemy.”

India ended its 2026 Asian Games campaign in Aichi-Nagoya with 85 medals – including 21 golds – and finished fourth in the medal table.
The haul also included 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, putting India ahead of Uzbekistan, which also won 21 golds but fewer silvers. China topped the standings with 169 golds, followed by Japan and South Korea.
The last day of the Games was critical for the country, with India collecting nine medals, five of them gold.
The hockey teams completed a rare double, with the women beating China 1-0 on Friday and the men defeating Malaysia 5-1 on Saturday. Both sides also secured qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
India also won both the men's and women's titles in cricket and kabaddi.
Golfer Pranavi Urs scripted history by becoming the first Indian woman to clinch an Asian Games gold medal in the sport.
Finally, archery and shooting were the biggest medal earners, with archery yielding five golds and shooting 15 medals in total. At 17 years of age, Kumkum Mohod was another breakout star for India, delivering a historic golden double in recurve on her Asian Games debut.
Despite many firsts, the total falls short of India's record haul at Hangzhou in 2023, where the contingent won more than 100 medals, including 28 golds.
Madhusudan "Mad" Sandhu, a Punjabi makeup artist and LGBTQ social media influencer, was shot dead by two unidentified men on a motorcycle in Amritsar on Saturday evening, local media reported.
Sandhu was attacked around 6 p.m. local time on Loharka Road, outside a car wash center. Bystanders rushed him to a hospital, where he died.
With over 200,000 followers on Instagram, he was known for speaking openly about makeup artistry, gender issues and LGBTQ rights. He ran a popular beauty salon and beauty academies in Amritsar.
Police registered a case based on a statement from his family.
"We have leads and will solve the case soon," Prabhjot Singh Virk, the city's Deputy Commissioner of Police (Investigation), said, according to local media.
While no arrests or motive have been announced, a social media post appeared soon after the shooting, claiming responsibility and accusing the victim of "spoiling" Punjab. This rhetoric was something Sandhu had regularly faced in his public life after being open about his sexuality.
Authorities said the post claiming responsibility was being looked into as part of the probe, NDTV reported.
Delhi Police have begun an inquiry into complaints by three women journalists who say they were sexually harassed by police personnel while covering protests against India's chief election commissioner .
In a statement on social media, police said the complaints were referred to the Crime Branch for a "fair and impartial enquiry."
The allegations emerged as police detained protesters near New Delhi's Jantar Mantar for a second day on Saturday, after over 700 people were detained on Friday. Demonstrators have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a mass voter-roll revision that has removed millions of names. The commission denies wrongdoing.
Kumar has not publicly commented.
In a video shared by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, one journalist alleged that an assistant commissioner of police groped her while she filmed the detention of student activist Neha Bora. Police have not publicly responded to the specific allegation.
Journalists and protesters gathered outside the Parliament Street police station demanding a report be filed, local media reported.
The Press Club of India expressed "shock and dismay" at the treatment of journalists and urged swift action. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi asked Home Minister Amit Shah to respond, noting that Delhi Police fall under his ministry.
Several student groups have called for a march from India Gate to Jantar Mantar on Sunday at 3 p.m. local time.
Meanwhile, opposition parties plan to march on the Election Commission on Tuesday, and the CJP has called for a mass mobilization in Delhi on October 10.
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, back with more from India this weekend.
Police are investigating sexual harassment allegations against its officers after scores of protesters were detained for a second straight day near New Delhi's Jantar Mantar.
Meanwhile, in the northern city of Amritsar, queer social media influencer and makeup artist Madhusudan "Mad" Sandhu was shot dead. Local authorities said a probe has been launched into his death.
Plus, India has wrapped up its Asian Games 2026 campaign with 85 medals, finishing fourth with a last-day gold rush.
For this and more, follow our live blog.
India offered a strong show on the last day of the Asian Games, but we aren't done with sports for the day. A FIFA international friendly match between India and Brazil is set to kick off in Kolkata later today.
As I sign off to watch that, we will now pause our coverage for the day. But we will be back tomorrow with more on the latest from India!
India's men's hockey team beat Malaysia 5-1 in Saturday's final to retain the Asian Games title, marking the first time the team has won back-to-back golds at the Games.
This came a day after India's women's team delivered one of the standout results of the Games, edging defending champions China 1-0 in Friday's final to end a 44-year wait for gold.
Forward Lalremsiami Hmarzote's goal in the 10th minute, backed by goalkeeper Savita Punia saving a penalty stroke from China's Zhang Ying before halftime, helped secure the win.
The victory was India's first women's hockey gold at the Asian Games since 1982 and also secured the team a direct qualification spot for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Pakistan summoned India's charge d'affaires in Islamabad on Saturday to lodge a "strong protest" over the alleged killing of two Pakistani civilians by India's Border Security Force (BSF) near the border in the Kasur district of Pakistan's Punjab.
Pakistan's Foreign Office said two unarmed civilians were killed and a third injured when BSF personnel opened fire in the Bedian sector on Friday, calling it "unprovoked and lethal force."
While there was no immediate comment from New Delhi, Indian media reported a conflicting account, saying the men were suspected of trying to enter the country.
Pakistan rejected any characterization of the men as "infiltrators."
The incident comes against a tense backdrop of a historically fraught relationship between the neighbors. It occurred a day after Pakistan's military publicly disputed an earlier Indian claim regarding a separate incident in Indian-administered Kashmir.
States in northern India continue to face an abysmal sex ratio at birth, leading to a shortage of women in places like Haryana.
This has led to thousands of women from poorer regions being brought to the state and sold as brides, giving rise to a lucrative human trafficking trade.

After posting 211-6 backed by Abhishek Sharma's 61 off 20 balls and a late effort from Tilak Varma and Shivam Dube, India restricted Pakistan to 192-6 despite a big knock of 96 off 51 balls from Hasan Nawaz.

articles.title_orig: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
articles.title_zh: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
articles.content_orig:
Last February, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck an Iranian elementary school, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. President Trump initially suggested that it could have been somebody else's Tomahawk: "Whether it's Iran or somebody else, the fact that a Tomahawk – a Tomahawk is very generic, it's sold to other countries, but that's being investigated right now," he said.
When Iran put out video as evidence that it was a U.S. missile, Hany Farid , one of the world's foremost experts on deepfakes, was contacted by several media outlets to determine if it was real or fake.
A professor at Dartmouth College, Farid is also co-founder of GetReal Security , a cyber security firm. "What was difficult about this case was you had very little to work on," he said. "We had a very grainy, shaky video. The missile is extremely small. And we had to reason about the physical plausibility of that missile striking the ground."
But he also had certain aspects that he could study scientifically, involving the speed of sound, the speed of light, and the size of the missile: "And those three things were enough for us to say that this is physically plausible," he said. "And this is the important part: all evidence led us to the belief that the video was authentic, and there's been no refuting of that."
But that's the world we live in: Reality itself, so perfectly mimicked by artificial intelligence, that even reality is suspect.
Farid said, "Here's the thing that makes me a little crazy, as a scientist in particular: I don't think you should be able to go into a court of law and say, 'Here is some evidence that is damning enough to put this person to death,' and then the judge says, 'Well, how do you know it's real?' And I say, 'Well, because the computer told me so.' This is not an answer
"And if I can't explain to you, to a judge, and to a jury, what is happening here – because the lighting, because the shadows, because the geometry, whatever it is – that's what we need to be able to do."
A case in point: Alex Pretti, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota. If you remember the scene last January 24, it was chaotic. Several ICE agents with guns surrounded Pretti.
Farid showed us a blurry photo of Pretti that was taken from the original video. "Somebody took this and 'enhanced' it," he said. According to Farid, the crispness of this "enhanced" image makes the scene feel "more real, but what it also did is when it enhanced it, it seems to have put a gun in [Pretti's] hand. If you go back to this video, the camera's panning a little bit and what's happening is, there's a shadow behind his hand on the street. And what the AI did is that it hallucinated this."
Farid says artificial intelligence has learned, "When you see photos like this with three men with guns, everybody's got a gun." And now, when you do Google searches for events like Pretti's killing, it shows the "enhanced" image.
By Farid's estimate, half of the content that's widely viewed on the Internet is fake, basically a toss of the coin. Much of it has its own sneering label: "AI slop." Footage of airplanes skidding on the tarmac, toddlers dancing a two-step, Elvis. "AI slop is a broad term that defines people generating content using AI just to grab eyeballs, video after video after video driving engagement," Farid said.
For the most part, Farid limits his examinations to the really serious stuff, the deepfakes. Even so, he's inundated. He said, "We're seeing deepfakes being weaponized in many, many different ways, from the creation of child sexual abuse material, to non-consensual intimate imagery, to full-blown state-sponsored disinformation campaigns, to what the North Koreans have done, [which] is to have their IT workers interview for jobs remotely. And they conceal their accent using AI. They can conceal their identity using a deepfake, where they change their identity from eyebrow to chin, cheek to cheek, in real time over a video call. They can conceal their geolocation. And they interview for jobs. I will tell you, just about every single Fortune 500 company has hired one or more of these, whether they know it or not.
"And now, the question you want to ask yourself is, what's next? Well, so one CEO said, 'Okay. No more virtual interviews. No more remote work.' That's insane. … We're gonna start flying people across the country? That can't be the answer. I mean it's exhausting. Let's be honest. I mean, if we're always looking at our shoulder over every email, every text message, every voicemail, every phone call, every video call? It's exhausting. I'm exhausted, and I do this for a living."
Asked if he has nightmares over deepfakes, Farid replied, "I look at content all day long. And usually the things I look at are not pleasant. I'm looking at bad things that involve horrific crimes, and when you view these things over and over and over again, they sit with you and you can't get them out of your head.
'And number two is, I don't want to be wrong. And five years ago I felt a lot more confident about our ability to distinguish real from fake. It's gotten harder. And then I worry more. I feel like the ground is constantly shifting," he said.
It builds – the stress, the pressure. After seven years on the West Coast, Farid returned to Dartmouth College, where he had previously spent 20 years on faculty. His wife, Emily Cooper, is also a professor there. The two of them bought a rural property in neighboring Vermont, where Farid mows acres of meadows, and cuts enough wood to feed their stoves through the winter. It's enough mowing and cutting to rinse some of those disturbing images away. It's isolated – there's no mail delivery, no garbage pickup –  but it's peaceful.
Certain work-related issues linger. Social media? Farid loathes it: "You can look at social media, at online platforms and say there is measurable harm coming to young kids, to adults, to seniors, across the boards. And I think we have been so mesmerized by these products which are, by design, meant to be addictive.
"I think we did an experiment on an entire generation of these young kids coming up, putting these devices in their hands. And now we've woken up and we're like, 'Oh, my God. This is terrible.' This generation right now has lower learning outcomes than any generation in history. Go to Palo Alto at the fanciest private schools where all the tech billionaires send their kids. There's no devices in those classrooms. They know."
That $17 billion settlement that Meta reached a few weeks back includes some safeguards, like a two-hour time limit for users under the age of 18. Farid thinks that's a start, but not nearly enough.
"The darkest vision I have is that everybody lives in their own information ecosystem, and nobody knows how to talk to each other anymore," he said.
On platforms where algorithms prefer fake to real content, Farid thinks all of us should stay off social media, or at the very least take those apps off our phones, to resist the temptation. As for those websites that promise to detect AI fakes, he says it's not that simple: "Here's what I think is next (and by saying next, I mean in the coming year), which is most of the deepfakes that we are seeing today have a human somewhere in the process. Somebody's hands are on the keyboard. There's still a human in the loop. But what's gonna start happening is AI agents are gonna start creating their own fakes."
And what is an AI agent? "An agent just has more autonomy, and what we have started to see is when you give it a problem to solve, it will find creative ways to do it, including creating a fake identity to interact with a human to get a human to do something and then it will lie about it," he said.
AI agents have been in the news recently for going rogue in testing trials, intensifying the global debate over AI safety and the very course of humanity . These are issues Hany Farid grapples with every day.

articles.title_orig: Week in review: Test your knowledge of notable news
articles.title_zh: Week in review: Test your knowledge of notable news
articles.content_orig:
Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
The Supreme Court will review a decades-old immigration law to decide whether ICE can detain undocumented immigrants indefinitely without bond.
From the end of the U.S. mission in Iraq to a botched execution in Tennessee, here are stories that made headlines this past week. Or skip to the end to test your news savvy with a quiz.
The Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump’s administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, at least for now.
The court granted the Justice Department’s emergency request to pause a lower judge’s ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The justices also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December.
More than 25,000 migrants were deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups.
Members of the Iraqi security forces stand guard Friday near the Victory Arch monument in Baghdad during preparations for Sovereignty Day celebrations marking the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces from Iraq.
BAGHDAD — U.S. forces ended their mission in Iraq on Wednesday, raising fears they will leave behind a security vacuum, further embolden Iranian-backed militias and give the Islamic State group an opening to regroup.
More than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed in chaos unleashed after U.S. forces toppled dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003, and 4,500 American troops died in the biggest U.S. war of the century so far.
Tehran views the pullout as a victory for its allied armed groups and a step toward its aim of driving U.S. forces out of the region. As the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran entered its eighth month, Iran said it received a U.S. response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed ceasefire.
Becca Good, wife of Renee Good, reacts Thursday during a news conference in Minneapolis, Minnesota, announcing the filing of federal civil rights lawsuits related to Renee Good’s death at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross.
The family of Renee Good, on Thursday announced the filing of federal civil rights lawsuits. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross shot and killed Good, 37, a U.S. citizen, on Jan. 7 during protests of deportation sweeps in Minneapolis. Her family sued the Trump administration, saying there had been “no accountability” for her killing.
Bills blocked: The Senate blocked legislation Wednesday requiring state utility regulators to consider whether large electricity users, including data centers, should bear the incremental costs of power infrastructure built to serve them, and a bill that would impose new controls on Congress members’ stock trades. Democrats said the bills didn’t go far enough.
Economy: U.S. gross domestic product increased at a 2.2% annualized rate, revised up from the previously estimated 1.5% pace, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis said Wednesday in its third estimate of second-quarter GDP.
Reflecting Pool: A judge Thursday permanently dismissed the Trump administration’s criminal case against Olympic canoeist David Hearn, who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Evidence suggests the damage was caused by flawed installation.
USPS: The U.S. Postal Service said Thursday it will take extraordinary measures to ensure the delivery of ballots for next month’s congressional elections, including extending hours at some retail branches, expedited handling, extra deliveries and special pickups of ballots.
Powell probe: The Federal Reserve’s Inspector General said Wednesday it found no grounds for a criminal referral or administrative misconduct tied to cost overruns in a central bank renovation project that drew scorn from President Donald Trump and an investigation of former Fed chief Jerome Powell.
Hijack attempt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that the co-pilot who tried to crash a passenger jet on its way to Israel the prior day had undergone Islamist radicalization.
Witness Damon Lawrence with the Roane County News on Wednesday recounts the attempted execution of Christa Pike at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. Pike had not been declared dead when the witnesses were asked to leave the room they were witnessing in.
Botched execution: Christa Pike, 50, received medical care in a hospital Thursday after surviving Tennessee’s two attempts to execute her with lethal injections, her lawyers said, renewing scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. It was the second botched execution in the state this year. Pike was sentenced to death in the 1990s after a jury convicted her of a murder she carried out as a teenager.
Cornell controversy: Cornell University agreed to an independent investigation into a suspected gang rape at a fraternity house, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Wednesday. Screenshots shared online of messages sent between suspected attackers and the school’s apparently lenient response to those involved sparked a firestorm of controversy.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks during a Friday news conference in New York City regarding an investigation into an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University.
Artificial intelligence: President Donald Trump released a document Tuesday that his administration cast as an accord on AI, which he said he and tech executives signed at a White House meeting. It urged controls in companies, including monitoring AI models in areas such as cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats to ensure models “do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”
Fat Bear Week winner bear No. 89 earned his “Backpack” nickname by riding on his mother, and former champion, Holly's back while crossing Brooks River in Katmai National Park and Preserve.
Fat bear: A male nicknamed “Backpack” emerged as the Fat Bear Week victor Tuesday, beating No. 910, an adult female, by 5,091 votes in the 12th edition of the annual beloved online showdown that celebrates bears’ pre-hibernation glow-up in Katmai National Park and Preserve. “A record-breaking more than 2.5 million votes” were cast over the week, organizers said.
$20 million: Funds Democrats say the government transferred from the Department of Homeland Security to air TV ads of President Donald Trump, including one that resembles one of his 2024 campaign ads. The Federal Communications Commission chair said Wednesday the ads aren’t improper.
Former special counsel Jack Smith is sworn in Tuesday as he appears before the Senate Judiciary Committee.
“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president or others,” former special counsel Jack Smith said Tuesday as he appeared voluntarily for his second public hearing before Congress on his investigations of President Donald Trump.

articles.title_orig: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.title_zh: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.content_orig:
‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift, anonymous access
They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.
Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”
The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.
Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.
While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”
The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
after newsletter promotion
Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”
But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”
While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.
It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

articles.title_orig: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
articles.title_zh: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
articles.content_orig:
Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that
‘S top sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru , was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online.
Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations ; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year , with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending.
That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin ) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks . But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as ) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand.
Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines ; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content.
Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks?
I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner . I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “ the next biggest influencers ”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one . “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another . “ I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke . I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world.
Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen.
Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

articles.title_orig: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has continued rallying for Republican candidates while visiting Ohio, proposing a defiant outlook on his party’s chances in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump told a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, claiming his Democratic opponents do not know what is happening.
Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, but the US president said Republicans would do better than critics expect.
“Just get out and vote,” Trump said as he rallied for US Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and other Republicans.
“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” he said.
Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds, with Trump’s popularity falling in recent months as higher petrol prices and those for other staples persist amid the US-Israel war ⁠⁠on Iran.
Husted, a Republican in a competitive Ohio race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, hopes the president can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip midterm elections.
Trump garnered more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.
Ohio petrol prices increased 35 percent over the past year to $4.16 per gallon (3.8 litres) on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which compiles data ⁠⁠on automobile travel. Trump’s trade policy with Canada has also led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3bn worth of Ohio exports, based ⁠⁠on 2025 figures, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported.
Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday’s rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war “on our terms” and, in the interim, he is “showing people that I’m fighting for lower prices”.
Trump extensively promoted his administration’s action on data centres, mainly those built for AI, during the rally, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Husted for an unsuccessful attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.
“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said, repeating his defence of data centres.
Data centres have become a hot political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.
The issue became especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centres to the Midwestern state as lieutenant governor.
The Republican-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats.
“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centres in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

articles.title_orig: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.title_zh: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.content_orig:
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.
Like the broader electorate , Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.
There are clear signs his party is paying the price.
A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.
Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%.
That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election.
Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference.
The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country.
The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections.
Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.”
“What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.”
But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012.
“Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said.
Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling.
His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference.
Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it.
Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue.
Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters.
A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024.
Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues.
“It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.”
“I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added.
Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family.
While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies.
Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough.
While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S.
Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans.
“There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added.
In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.
Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.
Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics.
She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.”
“They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added.
The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

articles.title_orig: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.title_zh: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.content_orig:
The Strait of Hormuz is going to remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker has said.
Iranian state-linked news agency Nournews, quoting ⁠Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, reported on Sunday that Washington made “some proposals through a mediator” days after the US replied ⁠to Iran’s diplomatic proposal.
The US should know “that the era of wasting time and dictating unilateral demands is over”, Ghalibaf said, adding Iran’s position remains “clear and definite”.
He emphasised that “the Strait of Hormuz will not open until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum are met”, and that Iran is “present on the military battlefield and will confront them with new surprises”.
He added that Iran was neither “excited” nor “intimidated” by the latest US proposals and would “both fight and negotiate”.
US President Donald Trump ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last week, hours after Iran put forward a roadmap to reopening the strait, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas is shipped during peacetime.
Last month, Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran in his speech on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
On Sunday, Iranian Foreign ⁠Minister Abbas Araghchi also said Iran is “serious about finding diplomatic solutions just as we are serious about defending ourselves”.
Speaking to foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran, Araghchi said Iran had clearly explained ⁠its conditions for reopening the strait and ⁠that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy and accept its proposal.
However, Araghchi warned that if the US takes military action again, Iran is “more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves”.
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Tehran used the UNGA platform last month to provide world leaders with its position on ending the US-Israel war on Iran.
He said the US has continued to focus on nuclear talks , while reopening the strait has been Iran’s main goal.
“We are at this stage mainly focusing on the strait, and our principal concern is to reach a solution and to have peace and stability restored within this waterway,” Baghaei said.
The Strait of Hormuz has been largely blocked and disrupted for more than seven months, since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, driving one of the worst maritime shipping disruptions in decades.

articles.title_orig: Co-pilot accused of trying to hijack Flydubai plane probably acted alone, Israeli sources say
articles.title_zh: Co-pilot accused of trying to hijack Flydubai plane probably acted alone, Israeli sources say
articles.content_orig:
The co-pilot accused of attacking his colleague on board the Flydubai flight to Israel and trying to seize the controls probably acted alone, Israeli sources told CNN.
International investigators are still working to determine a motive but an Israeli official said information from the inquiry suggested the suspect acted alone.
Another Israeli source said that, at the moment, Israel does not know of any link to a group or government. Both stressed this was their understanding so far.
The United Arab Emirates and Israel are both investigating the incident. The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing, is also conducting investigations.
The attorney general of the UAE, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot on board the flight had attempted to seize control of the plane by attacking his colleague with a crash ax – a piece of equipment required on most aircraft. The attorney general called the attempted hijacking a “terrorist act.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that Israel understands the suspect “underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” based on “personal information” collected during the suspect’s ongoing questioning. Netanyahu did not give any further details.
In the immediate aftermath of the attack, US President Donald Trump said that the suspect could be linked to Iran “based on what I’m hearing.” But he gave no other details.
Flydubai flight FZ1073 narrowly avoided disaster on its journey from Dubai, plummeting thousands of feet in a matter of minutes amid the attack on the plane’s captain.
Despite being wounded, pilot Captain Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door and signal his distress to passengers and crew, who bravely rushed into the cockpit to regain control of the aircraft.
Sources told CNN the suspect, named as Hamam al-Hammami, is an Omani national who had been removed from a previous job at Oman’s national airline last year following concerns about his extremist views.
A LinkedIn profile bearing the name Hamam al-Hammami said he worked at Oman Air for seven years, leaving in February 2025, before joining the Moroccan airline Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and departing in January 2026. One source told CNN that the profile belongs to the Flydubai pilot in Wednesday’s incident. The profile has since been deleted and CNN has reached out to LinkedIn for comment.
A post made to the LinkedIn profile on Wednesday, about nine hours after the incident, included a photo of the former leader of al Qaeda. It is unclear who published the posts or whether they were scheduled in advance.
Terrorist images found on Flydubai suspect’s social media
An Israeli official told CNN that al-Hammami had worked for Flydubai for only eight months.
Another source said the alleged assailant had previously worked for Royal Air Maroc. In a statement to the Associated Press, Air Maroc said the suspect trained with the airline for three months in 2025 as part of the pre-employment process but he was not selected.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also told CNN that it is investigating al-Hammami’s links to the country, and said an update will be provided when appropriate.
Questions remain over how a citizen of Oman, a country which does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel, was authorized to co-pilot a plane bound for Tel Aviv, despite Israel’s strict security regulations.
The names of all passengers and crew were provided to Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, Israel’s Tax Authority confirmed, adding that it is the Transportation Ministry’s responsibility to give answers on the matter of vetting. But a Transportation Ministry spokesperson told reporters on Saturday that its protocols do not include checking the names of flight crew members.
The incident has triggered criticism of the Israeli government, particularly its Transport Minister Miri Regev, who some opposition figures have called to be removed from office.
CNN’s Abbas Al Lawati, Kylie Atwood, Isaac Yee, Avery Schmitz, Thomas Bordeaux and Teele Rebane contributed to this report.
