articles.title_orig: How a senior thesis changed classrooms across America
articles.title_zh: How a senior thesis changed classrooms across America
articles.content_orig:
Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
Before fame came calling, these celebrities actually spent time working as teachers. ‘Hamilton’ creator Lin-Manuel Miranda worked as a substitute seventh-grade English teacher at Hunter College High School in New York before becoming famous for his songwriting and acting. Miranda had actuall…
Wendy Kopp was a senior at Princeton University in 1989, part of a cohort of the most recruited students in America.
She and her peers in what was widely called "The Me Generation" were being recruited by Wall Street, big banks, lobbying firms, consulting firms and Fortune 500 companies.
Kopp, who grew up in Dallas and went to good schools throughout her childhood, realized upon getting to Princeton and meeting people from less privileged backgrounds that not everyone had the same access to education she'd had. And, she said, she bristled at the characterization of her generation as selfish.
Wendy Kopp was a Princeton University senior when she conceived the idea for Teach for America. She wrote her thesis on the need to recruit top students from all disciplines to become teachers.
"I felt that was wrong," Kopp said. "I felt like I was one of many people I knew who were searching for ways to make a real difference, to tackle the inequities we saw in the country."
She did research. She wrote a senior thesis. And the idea she proposed in it led to more than 70,000 teachers being placed in classrooms across the U.S. and the world.
Kopp's thesis proposal eventually became Teach for America, which is now marking its 35th anniversary. But it almost never got past her paper.
A public policy major, Kopp had heard about a teacher shortage that was particularly acute in urban and rural districts.
"I thought, we can channel all this energy and talent," she said. "The first two years out of college, what if our future leaders were teaching in these schools instead of working on Wall Street?"
While some Teach for America alumni continue their careers as teachers, others go on to become administrators or work outside education.
She wrote her senior thesis proposing a teaching corps of non-education majors, young people who could hone their leadership skills in classrooms in places where they were needed most.
Kopp came up with a plan, a budget and a proposal for seed funding. Her peers’ reactions convinced her to see it through.
"It was magnetic," she remembered. "Everywhere I went, I'd send out the thesis in school districts and potential funders, and people thought it was a great idea, but no one thought it would work. They thought, college students will never do this."
Wendy Kopp is CEO of Teach for All after founding Teach for America and leading that organization for 24 years.
It was a bit more challenging to show non-education majors that they could be teachers.
"We asked, what better leadership opportunity is there straight out of college than to lead a classroom? To put kids on a positive trajectory, and build relationships and be part of a community?" Kopp said.
In three months, 2,300 students signed up, and by the end of the first year, 3,000 people had committed to teaching for two years.
Teach for America was a reality. And Kopp, after leading it for 24 years, is now CEO of Teach for All, a global education nonprofit.
Teach for America offers two-year, full-time, fully paid teaching positions in K-12 schools, as well as support from mentors and coaches. Recruits can teach in their own communities or elsewhere, with 40 regions nationwide. They receive health insurance and other benefits, and summer stipends, tuition grants and other aid are available. At the end of their two years, recruits may continue to work in classrooms or move on to other roles in education or outside it.
The program hasn't been without its critics: Some take issue with the model, arguing that placing inexperienced educators in under-resourced schools may not be the best way to fight education inequality. A 2022 National Education Policy Center blog lambasted the organization's training, leadership and positions on education reform.
But those inside the organization say it’s a powerful model that can change lives.
Aneesh Sohoni has been CEO of Teach for America since April 2025, but he's also an alum, having started teaching in Minnesota's Twin Cities in 2009. Initially, he'd planned to go to law school.
A political science major, Sohoni is the son of Indian immigrants and cognizant of the opportunities his parents' sacrifices made possible for him. He decided to give teaching a try.
"Once I met my students, I realized I wanted to do this for the rest of my life," he said. He met a lot of students who, like him, were the children of immigrants.
Aneesh Sohoni, right, is CEO of Teach for America. He'd once dreamed of becoming a lawyer but said, "Once I met students, I realized I wanted to do this the rest of my life."
"They had big dreams, but once I saw the obstacles in front of them, the lack of resources, you can't walk away,” he said.
He set out to be a teacher, but he learned from his students, too.
"Teaching is challenging, no doubt," he said. "And teaching in communities with the least access to resources is even more so. But there's nothing more rewarding than having this responsibility to work with students to set goals, to build relationships and to motivate them."
The support of other Teach for America recruits and the mentors was vital, Sohoni said.
"You're part of a community and you have an impact," he said. "Your typical 22-year-old college senior today came of age with social media and a pandemic and is graduating into a rapidly changing world. They crave community" and the opportunity to make a difference.
For some, what started as a two-year tryout became a passion and a calling. For Keon Davis, who teaches at Nuasin Next Generation Charter School in the Bronx, it's given him a feeling of community in his hometown.
Many of Davis' students come from low-income households, with many Black and Latino families.
"They come with a lot of emotions and needs that are outside of school," said Davis, who grew up in Harlem. He'd studied consumer behavior and marketplace studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison but was "dreading the real world. I had no idea what I wanted to do."
Teach for America recruits and trains people who studied for non-education careers and brings them into classrooms across the U.S.
Teaching, he said, "brought me community, growth, purpose, opportunity." It "pushes you into situations that will challenge you as a person and as a professional and make you a better person," he said.
Alejandro Diasgranados was a first-generation student at Virginia State, where he played football and studied physical therapy. He'd hoped for an NFL career, but an injury put an end to his dream. He didn't feel drawn to a career in physical therapy, though. A middle school teacher he'd kept in contact with suggested he go into teaching, which led to Teach for America.
Since its inception in 1989, Teach for America has trained more than 72,000 people to lead classrooms across the U.S. Some of them continue their teaching careers, while others apply the lessons they learned in other careers.
He started in Camden, New Jersey, before moving to Washington, D.C., where he's been for 11 years. He teaches second and third grades.
The job isn't without its challenges, he admitted: Seaton Elementary, where he teaches, is temporarily housed at Howard University, and its students speak seven different languages.
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, many of Diasgranados’ students lacked computers at home, so he got creative and started reaching out "to everyone I could." The persistence paid off when actor and daytime TV host Drew Barrymore presented the school with 250 laptops.

articles.title_orig: Chick-fil-A wants to stay a family business even as it expands in the U.S. and abroad
articles.title_zh: Chick-fil-A wants to stay a family business even as it expands in the U.S. and abroad
articles.content_orig:
With restaurants as far-flung as Singapore, Chick-fil-A has expanded far beyond its Southeastern stronghold in recent years, but CEO Andrew Cathy still wants the family-owned business to stay true to its roots.
Nearly five years ago, Cathy succeeded his father, Dan, as chief executive of the chicken chain his grandfather, S. Truett, founded. He took the reins as elevated inflation rocked the restaurant industry and a bevy of new chicken rivals looked to challenge Chick-fil-A's dominance. Since then, not much has changed — except for sluggish traffic across the industry as consumers have become more selective about their dining choices.
The challenging conditions have led to disappointing results for McDonald's , Popeyes, KFC and other restaurant competitors. While Chick-fil-A is not immune to these headaches, Cathy told CNBC that the chain's restaurants have not seen the same downturn.
"This has been a good year," the Atlanta-based Cathy said in downtown Manhattan before a planned activation to raise awareness for the chain's Shared Table hunger relief program.
"Our operators have done such a good job executing on the fundamentals and adding the hospitality to it," he added.
As a privately held business, Chick-fil-A does not report quarterly results. However, franchise disclosures reveal that the company's revenue in 2025 rose 14% to $10.3 billion, while its net income ticked up 1% to $1.05 billion. Its roughly 3,000 locations generated $23.92 billion in system sales last year, making it the third-largest U.S. restaurant by sales, trailing only McDonald's and Starbucks .
Chick-fil-A has no plans for an initial public offering or any other opportunities for outside investment. Cathy said the company plans to stick with its "calculated" and "conservative" growth.
But he may be underselling Chick-fil-A's recent expansion. It opened 179 restaurants last year and has launched in international markets like Canada, Singapore and the United Kingdom in recent years.
Staying private also has advantages, particularly as restaurant stocks have broadly struggled this year. Shares of Jersey Mike's have fallen nearly 28% since its initial public offering in July, while Dunkin' owner Inspire Brands is reportedly unlikely to go public this year unless the sector's performance improves.
"We're able to plan for the quarter century, and we don't have to plan for the quarter," Cathy said.
During Cathy's tenure so far, Chick-fil-A has pursued bold ideas for future growth, like a $1 billion international expansion plan and Daybright, a new beverage-focused restaurant concept created by its venture arm.
But the company is trying to balance those new strategies with its existing traditions.
"I look at driving this business like driving a race car — there's a reason that the windshield's bigger than the rearview mirror," Cathy said. "It's important for the rear view to be grounded on where you are, and there are things that we think about our purpose, our mission, that won't change, but everything else we have to be able to evolve and change."
Some tenets, like staying closed on Sundays, will never change. Others, like its restaurants' signature Southern hospitality, will evolve as diners change their ordering and eating habits.
Cathy said that Chick-fil-A takes a "human plus" approach to technology in its restaurants.
"We think about all these new things into the future, about how will people want to receive food in the future?" he said. "As you think about drone delivery and all the other kind of things that could be coming, it's a fun time in the industry, to think about all the possibilities of what we can do to make a better experience for our guests."
While Chick-fil-A is exploring opportunities to use artificial intelligence behind the scenes, he said that its restaurants will not pursue AI voice ordering in its drive-thru lanes, unlike many of its industry rivals. McDonald's, for example, said at its investor day in September that it plans to test Archy, its voice AI tech, to take orders in both English and Spanish.
"From our experience, we really want that hospitality to be human to human," Cathy said. "We're not gonna substitute that interaction with technology, because we feel like that hospitality is so important to create that warm environment for consumers."
Other restaurants are also refocusing on hospitality, hoping that the extra effort from employees will encourage customers to come back. Starbucks bought around 200,000 Sharpie markers so its baristas could write friendly messages on customers' coffee cups. Burger King has redefined its restaurant manager role into a "Your Way Champion," who greets diners and fixes botched orders. And starting Monday, McDonald's will begin its "Make It Golden" training program for franchisees and employees, which focuses on hospitality as well as food quality.
Chick-fil-A's long-standing focus on service has made it the fast-food leader in customer satisfaction for more than a decade, according to the annual American Customer Satisfaction Index. That reputation can also help the chain stand out from other dining options as consumers have grown more choosy about how they spend their money. Jersey Mike's recently toppled Chick-fil-A in the 2026 study , although Chick-fil-A's score was unchanged from a year ago.
Another enduring element of Chick-fil-A is its famously simple menu. But the chain has even been carefully expanding its offerings, typically through seasonal limited-time items like chicken and waffles or its Honey Pepper Pimento Chicken Sandwich. If a menu item is a "home run," as Cathy calls it, then Chick-fil-A might add it permanently, like its Pineapple Dragonfruit drink line.
"We're very careful about what we want to do, because we want to keep it really focused on unique Chick-fil-A items that they can only get at Chick-fil-A," Cathy said. "But we do want to bring in new flavors and profiles, and that's what we'll do with a lot of our seasonal items that we do, and we learn a lot from our customers about trying those things."
Other fast-food chains are trying to edge into Chick-fil-A's territory. In 2019, Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes sparked the "chicken sandwich wars" by releasing its own version. Chick-fil-A remains the dominant chicken chain in the U.S., with roughly a 43% market share as of 2024, according to Barclays. However, the chicken sandwich helped catapult Popeyes to the No. 2 spot, with about 11% share.
McDonald's could reignite the battle as it prepares to test hand-breaded chicken strips and sandwiches.
But Cathy said that he loves the competition.
"I'm grateful that there's competition in the chicken space, because that means we're in a good space to be," Cathy said. "Competition just makes us better .... What little details can we do to make that environment even more welcoming for customers?"
Chick-fil-A has also innovated outside its restaurants.
In 2017, the company created Red Wagon Ventures, named for the vehicle Truett used to sell bottles of Coca-Cola in his first entrepreneurial gambit at age 6.
"The lion's share of our time and effort is continuing to make sure that we're getting better and better at Chick-fil-A, but we do have a small team that's working and incubating some of these new ideas and thinking about what could be some things that could help us grow into the future," Andrew Cathy said.
Some of those ventures are based in the restaurant industry. Its experimental Little Blue Menu concept served traditional Chick-fil-A menu items along with burgers, pizza and onion rings; the chain will convert its final location into a traditional Chick-fil-A next year. More recently, the subsidiary opened Daybright , which serves coffees, smoothies, juices and doughnuts — but no chicken sandwiches or waffle fries.
Another Red Wagon Ventures bet is even further from Chick-fil-A. Last year, it launched Acrew Home Professionals, a home repair and maintenance business that nodded

Physicists smashed gold nuclei together at nearly the speed of light and found an unexpected pattern in the particles these collisions sprayed out. If confirmed, that pattern could help reveal how the hot soup of quarks and gluons that filled the universe in the first few microseconds after the Big Bang cooled and condensed into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary matter today.
In every collision, particles are flung out sideways; how hard they are flung, on average, varies slightly from one collision to the next. Physicists expected the size of these variations to change smoothly as they adjusted the collision energy. Instead, the variations dipped, shrinking and then growing again. This dip could be a sign of a long-sought "critical point," a special set of conditions at which nuclear matter changes the way it transforms from one form to another.
The signal, detected by the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, is strong enough that it is very unlikely to be a statistical accident. However, the researchers cautioned that the dip is a tantalizing hint, not proof of the long-sought transition. They published their findings Sept. 22 in the journal Physical Review Letters .
Protons and neutrons are made of smaller particles called quarks, which are held together by the " strong force " carried by particles called gluons. When heated or squeezed enough, protons and neutrons melt into a hot soup of free quarks and gluons known as a quark-gluon plasma. It's thought that this primordial soup of particles filled the universe in the first milliseconds after the Big Bang .
Physicists want to pin down how this soup-ification happened, by measuring the so-called equation of state of nuclear matter. "For water, it tells you how pressure, temperature and density are linked, and therefore when it freezes, boils or expands," study co-author Rutik Manikandhan , a postdoctoral physics scholar at The Ohio State University, told Live Science in an email. For nuclear matter, "it is the basic rulebook for matter under the most extreme conditions in nature, such as the cores of neutron stars," Manikandhan added.
The "critical point" is a key landmark in that rulebook "For water, it is the point where the boundary between liquid and steam disappears," Manikandhan said, and theorists have long suspected that nuclear matter has a similar point. At extremely high temperatures, matter melts smoothly and gradually into quark-gluon plasma, but at higher densities, the change may become abrupt.
The critical point would mark where one kind of transition turns into the other. Some recent calculations place this point within reach of RHIC's lower-energy collisions. "But all of this is still conjectured and there is nothing concrete yet, either from the experimentalists or theorists," Manikandhan said.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The work also matters for cosmology. "Because the matter we create in these collisions resembles the matter that filled the universe a few microseconds after the Big Bang , mapping how it behaves helps us understand how the universe evolved from a hot soup of quarks and gluons into the protons and neutrons that make up everything today," Manikandhan said.
The central part of the three-story STAR detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Scientists recently used the detector to study the conditions of the early universe, just milliseconds after the Big Bang.
To explore this territory, the researchers ran RHIC at a range of collision energies. The lower the energy, the more tightly the colliding matter was squeezed. For its lowest-energy runs, STAR used a "fixed-target" setup, in which a beam of gold nuclei strikes "a thin gold foil placed inside the detector," Manikandhan said, instead of a second, oncoming beam. This produces the densest matter RHIC can make.
Collision energies are measured in electron volts (the energy an electron gains when accelerated across 1 volt). That is a minuscule amount, so particle physicists usually work in billions of electron volts, or giga electron volts (GeV). One GeV is roughly the energy locked up in the mass of a single proton, according to Einstein's famous equation E = mc 2 . The team analyzed roughly 1 billion collisions at energies between 3 and 7.7 GeV per pair of colliding protons or neutrons. That is the bottom of RHIC's range, which reaches 200 GeV.
In each collision, the team measured how hard charged particles were flung sideways out of the fireball ‪—‬ a quantity known as transverse momentum. The researchers then looked for correlations between the particles. A correlation measures whether two things tend to change together. Here, the team checked whether pairs of particles from the same collision tended to both be flung harder than average, or both more gently. That reveals something about the fireball as a whole. If a fireball is slightly hotter, or expands more forcefully, all of its particles get an extra sideways kick together.
"Those correlations reflect how much the temperature and the flow of the fireball fluctuate," Manikandhan said.
Close to a critical point, the matter's heat capacity — the amount of energy needed to raise its temperature — is expected to shoot up. That makes the fireball's temperature harder to budge, so the correlations should weaken. "If the matter approaches a critical point or a phase change, we would expect to see those correlations change in an unusual, non-smooth way as we vary the collision energy," Manikandhan said.
That is what the team saw in the most head-on collisions. "Instead of changing smoothly with energy, the correlations show a dip," Manikandhan said. The researchers compared the data with a smooth trend anchored by earlier STAR measurements at higher energies. The dip departs from that trend with a statistical significance of 5 sigma, the standard physicists usually demand before treating a signal as real. It means that if the true trend were smooth, random scatter in the data would produce such a pronounced dip only about once in 3.5 million tries.
"A smooth trend is what you'd expect from ordinary nuclear matter, so a dip suggests something more interesting is happening at those conditions," Manikandhan said.
By contrast, a widely used computer simulation of the collisions, which contains no critical point, reproduced the overall trend but not the dip. Off-center collisions showed only a faint h

articles.title_orig: Russia to Intensify Strikes on Ukraine After Zelensky Interview
articles.title_zh: Russia to Intensify Strikes on Ukraine After Zelensky Interview
articles.content_orig:
Russia will intensify strikes on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday, responding to an interview with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in which he vowed increased attacks on Russian refineries.
The ministry said Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defense industry sites and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine.
Zelensky had told Reuters in an interview published on Saturday that Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians.
Russia has recently escalated strikes on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital, including hitting bridges across the Dnipro river. The intensifying campaign has seriously disrupted life for the capital's 3 million residents ahead of the bitter winter months.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its recent strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions were a response to what it described as attacks by Kyiv on civilian targets inside Russia.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians.

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s presidential vote pits Trump ally against incumbent Lula
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s presidential vote pits Trump ally against incumbent Lula
articles.content_orig:
BRASILIA— Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in the first round of a narrowly split election after a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of U.S. meddling.
Leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , 80, is seeking a fourth term, while Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro , hopes to return his father’s right-wing ⁠movement to power.
A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with U.S. President Donald Trump, while Lula’s reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil’s public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign has offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25. Surveys show Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro polling roughly even in a likely runoff.
Other candidates, including former state governors Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu ⁠Zema, have struggled to break through with the polarized electorate, even as Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are ​each rejected by ⁠roughly half of voters, polls show.
Flavio Bolsonaro has promised to seek amnesty for his father, who is serving a sentence of more than 27 years for plotting a coup after his narrow election defeat in 2022. Lula has cast the election as a choice between “democracy and denialism” and repeatedly warned of foreign interference.
The fallout ⁠from Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction last year has colored much of the campaign.
Trump, who called that case a “witch hunt,” imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, explicitly linking the ​tariffs to the trial ⁠of Bolsonaro after lobbying from the Bolsonaro family to pressure Brazil’s Supreme ‌Court to drop the charges.
This year, Trump levied new tariffs over alleged unfair trade practices. Lula has cast the move as an attempt to sway the election and portrayed the Bolsonaros as too eager to please Washington at Brazil’s expense.
Lula’s allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins. They point to a failed effort to ‌send US officials to Brazil in order to “discuss electoral integrity,” according to the US State Department.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that ‌Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s affairs.
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
The senator, who has pledged closer ties with the U.S. and Israel, welcomed the Trump administration’s designation of Brazil’s major gangs as terrorist groups, which Lula rejected.
Also in play is U.S. access to Brazil’s vast critical ⁠mineral reserves, key to Washington’s push to reduce dependence on China for those materials.
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil’s president may need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to just 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.
“Lula would likely preserve a state-led model with only modest spending restraint; Bolsonaro would likely pursue a more market-friendly agenda centered on spending cuts, privatizations, concessions, and a stronger fiscal anchor,” said Alberto Ramos, chief Latin America economist at Goldman Sachs.
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed ‌much of Brazil’s political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. ​The investigation has probed the banker’s ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to ‌the case by the federal police.
The senator has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising ⁠millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker’s connections to Moraes, seen by many as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis ⁠a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case is politically and electorally motivated for his conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
Lula has also tried to distance himself from a federal police investigation into his son ‌over alleged influence peddling, which his son denies.
On Sunday, voters ​will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers ‌have pushed to impeach Moraes.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment ​of former President Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races.

articles.title_orig: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.title_zh: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.content_orig:
An appeal for wars to end and for peace to be built. The Pope renewed this appeal following the recitation of the Angelus prayer he led from the window of the Apostolic Palace. As he did during his recent visit to Lourdes, France, he again urged everyone to pray the Rosary for peace and unity in the world, standing in solidarity with children who have already begun doing so through the initiative of the Aid to the Church in Need Foundation, âOne Million Children Praying the Holy Rosary.â
âI wholeheartedly thank all the boys and girls who are joining in this prayer in so many parts of the world.  Let us all follow their example, invoking the intercession of the Virgin Mary so that peoples may be freed from the scourge of war.  In particular, let us pray for the Holy Land and for the innocent victims of violence.â
The campaign began at the start of October with the Pope in the Vatican Gardens and will continue until October 7, the Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. This allows dioceses, parishes, schools, communities, and families on different continents to choose the day that is most suitable for dedicating to this particular intention.
Pope Leo then announced that, on the occasion of the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, Pope Francisâs post-synodal apostolic exhortation, a week-long gathering will begin next Wednesday, October 7.
It will be held in his presence in the Paul VI Hall, with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Episcopal Conferences, to take stock of the situation of families today. The gathering will include testimonies from bishops and married couples from the five continents.
It will be an opportunity to listen to the voice of the Church at a time of profound change and to find ways to renew and strengthen the choice of marriage, which in various contexts has experienced dramatic declines over the decades. The Pontiff described it this way:
âIt will be a time of synodal discernment for identifying the steps to be taken in order to proclaim the Gospel today among families and the younger generations.  I entrust this task to your prayers and, above all, the families who, with Godâs help, are a sign of hope and an inestimable treasure for the Church and for society.â
The Pope then once again held up Saint Francis as a model, as he had done during the catechesis, on the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis. He expressed his happiness at the many commemorative initiatives, particularly those held in Assisi with the participation of Italyâs highest state authorities. He also offered a special greeting:
âI also greet the amateur radio operators of Assisi and Foligno who spread Saint Francisâ message of peace.â

articles.title_orig: Pre-COP31: World leaders must show up for the Pacific through action, not just speeches
articles.title_zh: Pre-COP31: World leaders must show up for the Pacific through action, not just speeches
articles.content_orig:
As Pacific leaders, communities and civil society gather in Fiji and Tuvalu for the Pre-COP31 meetings, the expected absence of many world leaders must not become another excuse for climate inaction, Amnesty International said today.
The meetings come after an unusually hot European summer, with August 2026 becoming the joint-hottest month on record. Against the looming threat of a powerful El Niño, widespread wildfires, droughts, and floods, the new UN warning of the world rapidly breaching warming thresholds adds urgency to the need for decisive climate action.
“World leaders have spent years talking about the climate threats facing the Pacific. Now they must come to Fiji and Tuvalu, listen to Pacific communities and act. Rising seas are already eating away at people’s lands, livelihoods and cultures. Concern without action will not hold back the tide,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“Those who do not show up in person cannot evade their responsibilities. Their absence will not stop the seas from rising or erase the obligations of high-emitting countries towards communities paying the highest price for a crisis they did least to cause.
“An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.”
Fiji’s Environment Minister has said that the Pacific-led summit will proceed “with or without” major world leaders .
An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.
Amnesty International has documented how climate change is already harming human rights in Tuvalu, Kiribati and other Pacific Island countries . Rising seas, extreme heat, droughts and saltwater intrusion are threatening people’s rights to water, food, health, adequate housing and a safe future. Tuvalu contributes less than 0.003% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it faces some of the climate crisis’ most severe consequences.
During her visit to Tuvalu in 2025, Agnès Callamard witnessed efforts by communities and the authorities to reclaim land from the advancing sea and enable people to remain in their homeland.
“To any world leader who hesitates to confront the biggest crisis of our time, I say this: come to Tuvalu. Speak to people living with rising seas and extreme heat. Witness their daily struggle to adapt, protect their rights and push back against the impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. The reclaimed land in Tuvalu is not a tourist backdrop. It represents a country fighting for its survival,” said Agnès Callamard.
Students from the Pacific took the fight against climate change to the world’s top court, leading the International Court of Justice to issue a landmark Advisory Opinion in July 2025, which made it clear that governments have a legal obligation to protect human rights from climate change impacts.
“The Pacific should not have to plead for the world’s attention. Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative,” said Agnès Callamard.
“Governments must end fossil fuel use and expansion through just transitions that leave no one behind, tax big polluters and deliver scaled up grants-based climate finance, providing climate reparations and ensuring communities on the front lines of the climate crisis have the resources and power to determine their own futures. The Pacific is sounding the alarm. If the world fails to act here, it will fail everywhere.”
Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative
As President of Negotiations at COP31, Australia has a particular responsibility to stand with its Pacific neighbours and secure an ambitious, human rights-centred outcome. Australia cannot credibly claim climate leadership while continuing to support fossil fuel expansion that deepens the harms facing Pacific communities.
Based on Amnesty International’s recommendations ahead of COP31 , Australia and other governments must use pre-COP31 to advance three priorities:
“Pacific leadership has helped keep the fight for 1.5°C alive, but Pacific communities cannot carry the burden of global climate leadership alone,” said Agnès Callamard. “Australia must use its presiding role to turn Pacific demands into COP31 outcomes, starting with stopping the crisis at source through a just transition away from fossil fuels.”
Governments cannot deliver climate justice while excluding affected communities or silencing those who challenge harmful projects. Across the world, Indigenous Peoples, environmental human rights defenders and communities on the front lines of the climate crisis are resisting fossil fuel expansion and fighting for fairer, more sustainable futures. Yet many face harassment, surveillance, criminalization, violence and restrictions on peaceful protest.
Australia’s treatment of peaceful climate activists will be an important test of its climate leadership. There are also concerns about restrictions on freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly in Fiji.
Ahead of COP31, Amnesty International is launching a global campaign “ Protecting our Future: Environmental Human Rights Defenders Powering Just Transitions ” spotlighting environmental human rights defenders and the alternatives they are fighting for around the world. This includes the First Nations people in Australia , who are challenging offshore oil and gas exploration affecting their lands and waters.
The campaign will show what resistance, dignity and a people-powered just transition can look like when communities refuse to see their lands, waters and futures sacrificed for fossil fuel profits.
Australia and Fiji must ensure that civil society, Indigenous Peoples, affected communities and environmental defenders can participate, speak out and protest peacefully without discrimination, intimidation or reprisals.
“Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions,” said Agnès Callamard.
“COP31 must deliver more than promises. Anything less would betray our shared responsibility to uphold human rights and secure climate justice.”
Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions
The Pacific-led pre-COP31 meetings will take place in Nadi, Fiji, and Tuvalu from 5 to 8 October 2026. COP31 will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026.

articles.title_orig: Is a stock market correction coming? Most Americans think so
articles.title_zh: Is a stock market correction coming? Most Americans think so
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
This year has been a challenging one for Wall Street, but that hasn't seemed to slow the market down.
Despite oil price shocks, surging bond yields, and AI safety concerns, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has surged by more than 21% over the past six months. The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) has fared even better, up by nearly 30%.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
However, the question is not whether a bear market is coming, but when . Stock prices can't keep climbing forever, and at some point, the market is bound to take a turn for the worse. Preparing for that downturn, though, is simpler than you might think.
Right now is perhaps the most nerve-wracking part of the market's cycle. Stocks are still at record highs, but with so many headwinds challenging the market, it feels like we're waiting for the other shoe to drop.
Nearly 50% of investors believe stock prices will fall in the next six months, according to the latest weekly survey from the American Association of Individual Investors. If you're one of them, it can be tempting to get out of the market now while prices are still high. However, history says it's actually more lucrative to stay the course.
The market often behaves unpredictably in the near term, and it sometimes continues to surge against all odds. In 2023, for instance, strategists at Deutsche Bank warned there was a "near 100%" chance that a recession would begin in the next year, emphasizing that a soft landing would be "historically unprecedented."
Three years later, and not only has that recession not materialized yet, but the S&P 500 has surged by nearly 82%. The investors who capitalized on these returns were those who continued buying even when the future looked bleak.
To be clear, this doesn't mean that the next three years will look similar to the last three. But despite all the warning signals, the market could still have plenty of steam left before the next downturn arrives.
The smartest move investors can make right now is to buy quality stocks and prepare to hold them for at least a few years. The longer you can hold your investments, the less likely you are to lose money -- even if the market crashes right after you buy.
Say, for example, you invested in the S&P 500 in late 2007. The market was on the verge of the Great Recession, and throughout the next two years, the S&P 500 would lose more than 50% of its value. Yet over the next decade, the index surged by more than 100%.
This trend holds up throughout history, too. Between 1919 and 2025, every single one of the S&P 500's rolling 20-year periods has ended in positive total returns, according to analysis from Crestmont Research. No matter how severe the short-term volatility, the market has always managed to thrive over time.
Now, could you have earned more by only investing during the market's low points? Of course. But it's impossible to identify the market's bottom in the moment, and if you wait too long, you risk missing out on the valuable recovery period.
While it's certain that another downturn will eventually arrive, no one can say exactly when. Rather than waiting for just the right moment to buy or sell, history suggests staying in the market is the more lucrative option.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread
articles.content_orig:
Most counties don’t have their own health agencies, and some specific population groups have low vaccination rates
Pennsylvania is bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials concerned that it’s “only a matter of time” until the disease spreads beyond the outbreak’s epicenter.
Last week the state reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The outbreak comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by increasing vaccine skepticism, especially due to the power and influence of controversial health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr .
Contributing to the challenge is that Pennsylvania is one of the few US states where its counties mostly lack their own health department, with only seven of its 67 counties having their own.
Lancaster county, which doesn’t have its own health department, has seen the highest amount of cases, at 381, believed to be mostly among the Amish or similar religious groups who have historically low rates of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine uptake. Health officials, doctors and other members of the community in the county are now attempting to establish its own health department to better tackle the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin , the director of Chester county’s health department, said that her county, which has the third highest number of cases, at 83, is preparing for an influx of cases from neighboring Lancaster.
“We have a very long border with Lancaster county, and these types of disease don’t care about borders,” Franklin said. “It’s going to keep going and find a person who isn’t vaccinated. We’re operating with the assumption that the disease may jump and spread to non-Plain [Amish] community members. Our goal is to prevent that, but we assume that it may happen.”
She added that although many Amish people have not been vaccinated, it’s not because they are anti-vaxxers, but rather because “they were either unaware of it or they don’t seek out healthcare as frequently as other residents”.
She added: “But they’re willing to have the conversation and make a decision on what’s happening today. They’re not making decisions based on the myths out there, but because their neighbors are impacted.”
Amid active surveillance of measles cases, contact tracing and setting up community vaccination centers, the county is also working to dispel misinformation some of its residents have regarding the safety of the vaccine.
“We have people in key positions saying it isn’t an outbreak, it isn’t a problem. We have people who approach our nurses and say that they were told the vaccine will make them sterile, or that there’s a microchip within it,” Franklin said.
But for Franklin, the fact that Chester county is one of the few counties to have its own health department is a clear advantage in the race to stop the spread of the disease.
“By having our own health department [it] means that we already have the infrastructure in place, and we prepare for these things all year round,” Franklin said. “With the number of counties [the state has] to provide support to, they can’t possibly know all the key partners in a geographical area.”
She added: “The state has a finite set of employees, while I can pull my employees away from their normal jobs and say we need help with this. We live here, we know it, and we’re working with the communities and the organizations who know us. I think every county needs a health department, but we’re just not set up that way in Pennsylvania while other states are.”
Dr Richard Lorraine, the medical director of Montgomery county’s office of public health, said that it is a “matter of time” before the third most populous county in Pennsylvania will begin to see measles cases.
“We recognize that essentially it’s all around us, and so a big focus for the county is immunization,” Lorraine said. “It’s the best preventative measure and where the county is focusing its efforts on.”
after newsletter promotion
Working closely with community organizers, Lorraine said the county was making sure that every resident was able to be vaccinated regardless of their insurance status.
“Because we are a public health agency, our mandate is to provide for members of our population for the most part who are underinsured, and there’s a very high percentage who aren’t insured,” Lorraine said. “And through our partnership with pharmacies we’re able to open these clinics for everyone. So whether you have insurance or if you don’t, we can work it out so that someone is able to administer a vaccine.”
Lora Werner, the director of the Delaware county health department, said that her agency is facing several challenges in protecting residents from the virus.
Among them was the collapse of Crozer Health, Delaware county’s largest healthcare system, due to bankruptcy last year.
“They were a huge provider of pediatric care,” Werner said. “And although we do have a high vaccination rate across Delaware county, there are pockets where they aren’t as good.”
For Werner, the newly established local health department has been a gamechanger for promoting public health initiatives in the county.
“We are the newest health department on the block, and we’re so passionate about the fact that we’re now here and can serve our residents,” Werner said. “We’re deeply integrated into the social networks.”
She added: “Creating a new department was very challenging, and we’re a very odd state in this regard,” Werner said. “If you want to have one you need to have a referendum to establish one. But it’s not required, so we have a mishmash of the counties that have taken that step and those that have not.”
The Guardian has approached the Pennsylvania health department for comment.

articles.title_orig: In Shanghai’s ‘Science City,’ China’s ascendant biotechs make their pitch to the world
articles.title_zh: In Shanghai’s ‘Science City,’ China’s ascendant biotechs make their pitch to the world
articles.content_orig:
This story is republished from STAT , the health and medicine news site that’s a partner to the Globe. Sign up for STAT’s free Morning Rounds newsletter here .
SHANGHAI — The biotech executives appeared triumphant.
It was a balmy, overcast Sunday here in the glimmer-and-glass “Science City” district, and the four leaders were on stage at the ballroom level of the five-star Hilton, joking about how much faster, cheaper, and more efficient drug development was here in China than anywhere else — certainly than the United States. (And God help Europe.)
Zhui Chen, cofounder of the now $6 billion Shanghai-based biotech Abbisko, recalled running a trial on a drug licensed to the German pharma Merck KGaA. Abbisko’s trial finished in 11 months, so quickly that Merck executives asked if Abbisko could train their staff.
For two years, American labs and board rooms have been riven with excitement and anxiety over the vertiginous rise of Chinese biotech. Almost overnight, it seemed, a half-century of American dominance in life sciences had evaporated. Big Pharma executives in New Jersey and New York scrambled to license drugs from Chinese companies few American scientists had ever heard of, hoping to find the next blockbuster to fill their balance sheet. Founders and investors in South San Francisco and Kendall Square watched their companies get passed over — or fold altogether — and wondered if they had a future.
To plant its own flag, Jefferies, the New York investment bank, convened its first Shanghai-based conference. The rationale was simple. The largest US life science conference is J.P. Morgan’s San Francisco summit. The largest European conference is held by Jefferies in London. China is still up for grabs.
On the main stage, panelists debated artificial intelligence, obesity, geopolitical tensions, American innovation versus Chinese execution, and the best way to commercialize a drug. Many pleaded for collaboration, not competition.
Executives walked through their pipelines in English, flashing antibody drugs in full Revlon counter variety. Local representatives from hulking multinationals like GSK, Merck, and Sanofi roamed the halls, scouting potential prospects. A contingent from SK Biopharmaceuticals, the Korean pharma, filled an elevator.
Even longtime veterans of the drug industry here struggled to make sense of what they’re seeing.
“It’s really blowing like everyone’s mind, right?” said Betty Huang, who helps spearhead Chinese business development for the German pharma Bayer.
Behind closed doors, a new wave of deals were coming to the fore. Cui Cui, Jefferies’s head of health care research for Asia, told local media that investors had traveled from Brazil and South America. The Shanghai conference was appended to a broader Asia tour, and Cui said she had met with representatives from a Texas teachers’ pension fund in Korea who “are very interested in China” — though they can’t invest for “various reasons.”
Venrock and other US VC firms had staff on site, talking trades and scoping out local operations. One US-based investor was trying to decide if they needed to hire someone in the region full time. Michael Garrow, chief investment officer of HS Group, a Hong-Kong based investment firm that backs specialized hedge funds, was meeting with portfolio managers to see if it was time to reinvest. Could he find “the RTW or RA Capital of Asia?” he said, naming prominent US health care funds.
A decade ago, health care-focused firms had popped up and flamed out in Asia. But now, there seemed to be “real innovation,” he said.
It was a well-timed summit. Two days before kickoff, the Chinese government issued its latest five-year-plan for biotech. By 2030, it wrote, Chinese drug developers should have at least five blockbuster drugs. One fourth of all first-in-class drugs should come out of China.
Bold, to say the least. Today, Chinese drugmakers have one or two blockbusters.
It’s hard, though, to see the latest frenzy of dealmaking and see anything but a diagonal line pointing up. The numbers vary, depending on which bank, consulting firm, or analyst you trust. But Chinese-designed drugs now make up about a third of the world’s pipeline and draw more than half of all licensing or collaboration deals, as measured by total dollar value.
Morgan Stanley seems to be a believer, projecting Chinese-designed drugs will account for 35 percent of all Food and Drug Administration approvals by 2040, compared to 5 percent today. So is Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla, who warned an Atlantic Council audience recently that the gravity had already shifted.
“I don’t want to lose the superiority of the US biopharma to the Chinese, which I see that happening in five years,” he said. “I don’t want that to happen. But we are putting 80 percent of our energy to think how to slow them down rather than 80 percent of our energy to see how we can become better than them.”
The Chinese government has been trying to steward biotech here for years, with mixed success. In the 2000s, large pharmas like GSK and Novartis set up R&D centers here, but most of them ultimately pulled back, with little to show for the lucre spent.
Most observers point to 2015 as the pivotal moment. The government started speeding review of new trials and approvals and brought its clinical trial system in line with international standards. In 2018, the Hong Kong stock exchange allowed unprofitable companies to go public, thus boosting biotech fundraising and VC returns.
Meanwhile, Chinese contract research organizations and manufacturing companies, like Wuxi AppTec, grew remarkably efficient, in part by working with American companies. Local scientists learned drug development inside these CROs, or the local divisions of Big Pharma. Or they trained abroad and came home.
American companies still work with the CROs, which are tightly woven into the ecosystem here. “A Chinese scientist who is using a CRO can just ride a bike and supervise them on how to do the science,” said one prominent Chinese biotech venture capitalist. “Unlike sitting in Boston, where you send an email and they respond a day later.”
Meanwhile, companies can enroll patients faster because large hospitals attract thousands of patients for care.
The result is companies that can engineer molecules every which way with ruthless efficiency and put them into early development on the cheap. After mastering generics, companies moved on to me-too-drugs, then me-better, and now are competing with US companies to develop more novel compounds.
Today, the old GSK building is occupied by Abbisko, beside other local pharma companies in an office park that features a KFC and Starbucks. Their scientists, typically making around 50 percent of what a US scientist would make, contribute to a system that is about 50 percent to 70 percent faster than the rest of the world in developing trial-ready molecules and then two to five times faster at recruiting patients for late-stage trials, per McKinsey estimates .
Ying Huang, who steered the Chinese-founded startup Legend Biotech as it beat out US competitors to develop a powerful cancer cell therapy Carvykti, sat on the same panel as Chen, the Abbisko cofounder. He said his distressed Boston colleagues complain that office and lab space in Kendall Square is vacant and they can’t get funding.
“We all know that this is the competition,” said Huang, who lives in New Jersey and now runs a startup licensing molecules out of China. “Whoever is more innovative, whoever is more efficient, will get investment.”
For all the fanfare, few thought — or at least would say — that the US biotech industry would wither away. Kendall Square would survive, assured Eric Liu, managing director of Banyan BioInnovations, a new China-focused offshoot of the life sciences investment bank Locust Walk.

articles.title_orig: She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter
articles.title_zh: She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter
articles.content_orig:
🎧 Prefer to listen to this story? Hear it in the NPR app .
NPR Ukraine producers Polina Lytvynova and Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.
When the Fox News Channel hosted hundreds of advertisers and industry executives at the ornate Hammerstein Ballroom in Manhattan two years ago, the network centered attention on a tragic yet heroic figure: the war correspondent Benjamin Hall.
"From Ukraine to the Middle East, and here at home, the dedicated journalists of Fox News are trying to inform Americans, even in the most perilous of circumstances," Hall proclaimed .
Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall is treated for injuries that he sustained while reporting in Ukraine in March 2022. Fox News / Screenshot by NPR hide caption
Hall knows peril all too well. In the first weeks of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a strike by Russian forces hit the car in which Hall's team had been traveling outside Kyiv.
Hall had nearly died. He lost his right leg below the knee, most of his left foot and part of an eye.
Two years after the attack, Hall stood center stage on prostheses, in a suit that ended just above his knees. He entered to a standing ovation.
Hall is interviewed about his book, Saved: A War Reporter's Mission to Make It Home , on Fox & Friends on March 10, 2023. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
"These stories, they need eyes on the ground," Hall said. "They need a human perspective. They need us to bear witness."
Though gravely injured, Hall was the lucky one. The strike killed all four people who traveled with Hall that day:
The two Ukrainian soldiers who served as guides. Pierre Zakrzewski, a beloved Fox war videographer. And Oleksandra Kuvshynova, known as Sasha. The 24-year-old Ukrainian had just joined the team as a producer and interpreter.
Oleksandra "Sasha" Kuvshynova and Pierre Zakrzewski. Fox News / Screenshot by NPR hide caption
Fox has described the deaths as tragic and honored the fallen. Yet two multimillion-dollar lawsuits against the network blame it for what happened.
One of those lawsuits has been filed by Kuvshynova's parents, who also squarely blame Hall. In their first joint interview about the tragedy, they tell NPR they are speaking out to honor their daughter's life and document what they contend is the injustice of her death.
Andriy Kuvshynov and Iryna Mamaysur hold a portrait of their daughter, Oleksandra Kuvshynova, in 2024. Paula Bronstein for NPR hide caption
Two high-risk security advisers who worked for Fox News in Ukraine bolster the family's claims. In separate interviews with NPR about what happened, they say Fox News and its star correspondent ignored repeated and urgent warnings to stay away from the danger zone outside the city limits of Kyiv.
"If you took Benji out of the equation, this never would have happened," Aaron King, one of those security advisers, said. The other adviser, Shane Thomson, has joined the Kuvshynovs' lawsuit, alleging Fox scapegoated him for the tragedy.
This story is based on 15 interviews and a review of hundreds of pages of legal documents, as well as Fox's own broadcasts. Fox News, citing the ongoing litigation, declined NPR's repeated and detailed requests for interviews with Fox officials, news executives and lawyers. The network also did not make Hall available for interviews for this story. It additionally declined to respond to specific questions raised for this story.
Shane Thomson was a high-risk security contractor for Fox News during the beginning of the war in Ukraine. He has joined a lawsuit against the network. Sam McQueen for NPR hide caption
Yet one of the most revealing witnesses to Hall's character is Hall himself. He wrote a memoir, published a year after the attack, in which he acknowledged increasingly embracing risk as his career and ambitions progressed. The same year, he also presented his story in a Fox documentary.
Fox and its founder, Rupert Murdoch, have faced controversies, scandals and litigation before. Often, accusations center on the network's right-wing ideology, Murdoch's own political agenda or their relentless pursuit of profits.
Two words define the underlying allegations in the Kuvshynovs' wrongful death lawsuit against Fox and Hall: ambition and negligence.
Covering any armed conflict by definition involves peril. Hazards are often ambiguous; the boundaries of battle zones are fluid. Combat journalists for many news organizations, including NPR , have been killed.
But the Kuvshynovs and their legal team say what happened to their daughter was preventable — and foreseen. "This was a very avoidable danger that they were specifically warned about, as to [the] exact time and place that they could not go," charges Stephen Humphreys, a lawyer for the Kuvshynovs and Thomson.
American lawyer Stephen Humphreys is representing Kuvshynova's parents in their lawsuit against Fox News. He is seen in Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2024. Paula Bronstein for NPR hide caption
In court statements in the Kuvshynovs' suit, Fox acknowledges the tragedy of the deaths of Kuvshynova and Zakrzewski. But the network counters the plaintiffs' claims on technical and legal grounds.
In declining comment for this story, Fox pointed NPR to a statement released in March 2024, when the lawsuit was filed.
"While we understand the grief and continue to mourn the loss of both Pierre Zakrzewski and Sasha Kuvshynova, we will respectfully defend against the inaccurate claims within this lawsuit," Fox said.
"The safety of our journalists has always been our number one priority and we are immensely grateful to the Fox News journalists who have covered the war in Ukraine and we remain committed to reporting from the region," the statement continues.
It wasn't clear that Hall would get to Kyiv in early 2022.
A dual British-U.S. citizen, Hall was inspired by his globe-trotting family's past. He wrote in his memoir that at the outset of World War II, his dad's family was in the Philippines. Japanese forces took Hall's grandfather prisoner and executed his grandmother and other relatives. U.S. troops rescued Hall's father, then just a boy.
In chronicling combat, Hall wrote, "I saw a lot of death, had guns pressed against my head, dreamed horrific dreams — all of it an echo of what my father endured in Manila."
In his 20s, Hall pinged from one hot spot to another, freelancing for outlets like Vice and Esquire , and Fox.
The first time Hall saw a man die was in Misrata, Libya, in 2011. He had a choice, he recounted in the memoir, titled Saved : He could turn away or, perhaps, "invade the dignity of those moments in order to 'get the story.'"
"I did not have the time to consider all the moral angles. I could either keep filming, or stop filming, and I chose to keep filming," Hall wrote. He added that he had just escaped being killed too.
Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst attends the 2026 White House Correspondents' Dinner on April 25. Paul Morigi/Getty Images hide caption
Back in London, Hall registered that he had undergone a profound transformation. "I learned that I could control my fear, even bury it, and keep moving forward into danger," Hall wrote. "I learned that the hellishness of Misrata was not enough to stop me from going to combat zones.
"And I learned that my normal civilized life would never be the same again. No — this was who I was now."
Years later, his colleague Trey Yingst would call Hall "the gold standard" for war zone reporting for the network.
But there was at least one early red flag. In a sworn affidavit for the Kuvshynovs' lawsuit, former Fox News international producer Phil Ittner said he had previously lodged a formal internal complaint that Hall's behavior in Syria had placed colleagues in danger.
"Ben Hall was addicted to the adrenaline rush of taking risks," Ittner wrote in the affidavit. "I worried that he put his career promotion ahead of the safety of the crew working with him." He called for Hall to be pulled from the field. Instead, Ittner wrote in the affidavit, Fox ne

Internationally acclaimed mentalist Steve Taubman will bring his show “Mind Magic: A Night of Laughter and Astonishment” to the Alamo Theatre in Bucksport on Thursday, Oct. 15, at 7 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
articles.title_zh: Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthis have said they attacked an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government intensifies.
In a statement posted on X on Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had carried out a “military operation with ballistic missiles and drones” that targeted Aramco in Riyadh.
He claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and “led to fires breaking out” at the site. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising near an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday.
Later on Saturday, Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media that the Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh were “misleading”.
Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, said the attacks targeted “at least 260 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled 44 military vehicles”.
Late last month, the Houthis said they had attacked Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Red Sea port on Saudi Arabia’s west coast.
Saudi Arabia said at the time it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired towards Taif and Yanbu and reported no damage to Aramco sites.
Earlier this week, the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis attacked a power station in the Muslim holy city of Medina on Tuesday.
The fighting has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July.
In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since fighting restarted.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title_orig: The Guy Behind The Big Short and Moneyball Is Back to Take On Elon Musk and DOGE. It’s a Roller Coaster.
articles.title_zh: The Guy Behind The Big Short and Moneyball Is Back to Take On Elon Musk and DOGE. It’s a Roller Coaster.
articles.content_orig:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
Michael Lewis’ new book, Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State , is a roller coaster. It alternates between the heartening stories of stellar federal civil servants, competent people who sacrifice high-paying jobs in the private sector to make their corner of the government work, and accounts of the early destruction wrought by the Department of Government Efficiency and its phalanx of sullen , Elon-worshipping idiot boys . The highs are very much what readers expect from Lewis, a journalist whose ability to make everything from bond trading to subprime mortgages both intelligible and exciting has routinely landed his books ( Moneyball , The Blind Side , The Big Short ) on the bestseller lists. The lows are blood-pressure-spiking accounts of 20-year-olds with no professional experience to speak of (as Lewis puts it, “only just now grokking the fact that the United States government had three branches”) blithely demanding access to tranches of sensitive data and firing people whose jobs they couldn’t begin to understand.
“Blocker” is a label Elon Musk liked to slap on anyone attempting to stand in the way of his clueless, largely illegal, and entirely ineffective campaign last year to cut government spending. Blockers offers six portraits of federal workers accused of such obstruction, from the head of security at the United States Institute of Peace—an independent, nonpartisan institution over which DOGE had no legal authority—to an official at the IRS who had to resort to locking herself in a darkened conference room to avoid Gavin Kliger , a diminutive, capricious DOGE goon who wanted her to give him confidential information on 7 million taxpayers. Then, to mix it up, Lewis includes a final chapter, a wild card of sorts, suggesting what DOGE might have been if the people involved had had any decency at all.
By Michael Lewis. W. W. Norton & Company.
Slate receives a commission when you purchase items using the links on this page.
    Thank you for your support.
Lewis adroitly fashions each worker’s story as a different flavor of narrative. That USIP chapter reads like a political thriller. A later chapter profiles Alexander Maranghides, a naturalized citizen originally from Greece who worked for the National Institute of Standards and Technology, specializing in firefighting in the wildland–urban interface. Maranghides’ story is a quest saga, the tale of a man determined to understand a type of disaster that had gone relatively unstudied. (Previous fire-protection engineers mostly concentrated on either fires inside buildings or wildfires.) As with the other civil servants Lewis profiles, Maranghides devoted his life—including many unpaid hours—to his job, until the appointment of the vapid Howard Lutnick as secretary of commerce, the Cabinet position overseeing the NIST. The second Trump administration cut the institute’s budget by half, and Lutnick made no protest, focusing instead on jostling for face time with the president or arranging for his personal butler “to serve him a full-on fancy restaurant meal complete with all the silverware, while the people briefing him looked on,” Lewis writes. Maranghides retired in his late 50s, taking with him a treasure trove of expertise on the kind of fire that destroyed much of the Pacific Palisades last year and that increasingly poses a threat to the wholly unprepared East Coast, as well.
That butler detail is pure Lewis. He has an unfailing eye for the image that nails the emotional undercurrent of a scene, and Trump’s host of craven apparatchiks offers him plenty of those. He playfully frames his chapter on the forced retirement of Francis Collins—former head of the National Institutes of Health and perhaps the best-known public official profiled in Blockers —as a hard-boiled murder mystery. Seeking to identify the Trump administration figure who had Collins “whacked,” Lewis hams it up with lines like “The remaining three suspects rolled around Francis’s insides like last night’s undercooked chicken.” But when he describes the day Collins was compelled to leave the job he loved, Lewis writes that Collins called “his wife, who picked him up to drive him home. He left carrying a small cardboard box with a few pictures, a spare necktie, some ramen noodle packages, and a mirror made by children in NIH clinical trials, all of whom had died. He’d bought it at an auction to raise money for a children’s hospital.” Although personally modest, Collins has an impressive record. He headed the Human Genome Project and was instrumental in identifying the gene responsible for cystic fibrosis. The “small cardboard box,” in this light, makes for an especially poignant touch at the end of an extraordinary career.
Collins’ story also underlines the appalling reckless of the second Trump administration’s hatchet work. Russell Vought—director of the Office of Management and Budget and fingered by Lewis as a likely suspect in Collins’ “whacking”—has a daughter with cystic fibrosis. “As he considered his child,” Lewis writes, “Vought had to know—and might have allowed himself to care—that he owed her life to Francis Collins and, more broadly, to work sponsored for fifty or more years by the National Institutes of Health.” When he got the ax, Collins asked for a pass that would allow him to continue working at his lab at the NIH (without pay), researching a disease that causes premature aging in children. He was told by a Trump flunkey named Matt Memoli that if he didn’t clear out entirely, he’d be publicly blamed for funding research at a lab in China where the COVID virus was allegedly “cooked up.”
Although Lewis doesn’t tout it, this story is something of a scoop, as Collins has previously been circumspect about his reasons for retiring. Similarly, his reporting reveals that Melanie Krause—the former acting IRS commissioner who has been portrayed as courageously resigning from her post when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went behind her back to sign a memorandum agreeing to unlawfully share IRS date with Immigration and Customs Enforcement—was, in fact, a weak-willed quisling. Krause complied with Gavin Kliger’s demand that she fire the service’s head of human resources, who had refused to send an email terminating all probationary employees under the false accusation of poor performance. Krause also tried to get another IRS official to facilitate the handover of taxpayer data to the Department of Homeland Security so that she wouldn’t be responsible for it herself. That official, Kathleen Walters, the hero of the IRS chapter—a twisty tale of palace intrigue, bureaucracy-style—resigned instead.
The catastrophic waste of driving such gifted and committed civil servants out of the government will hurt the United States for decades to come, as will their current, incompetent replacements, whose sole qualification is their loyalty to Donald Trump. No sooner does Lewis buoy his readers’ spirits with a portrait of a man uncannily capable of resolving disputes between government managers and their employees’ unions (“It’s hard to explain the connection between Tim’s job and the speed with which you get your tax refund,” he quotes one source saying. “But there is a connection. Tim is needed for the government to work”), than he recounts how the stupidity of Musk’s infamous “five bullets” email drove the guy out.
One of the few consolations in this sorry spectacle is the likely success of Blockers, and the fact that the misdeeds of such DOGE toadies as Kliger, Marko Elez, and Nate Cavanaugh, as well as the spineless officials who submitted to them, have become a matter of more public record. ( Additionally, some of them are being sued .) Let their names be a curse, and widely published in connection with their vandalism.
